ResearchDossier.topic: New Year's resolutions are 4,000 years old
ResearchDossier.summary: Around 2000 BC the Babylonians celebrated the new year in a 12-day festival called Akitu, making promises to return borrowed farm equipment and pay debts. The Romans adopted the custom; after the Julian calendar (46 BC) they began each year with promises to the god Janus. An early instance of the phrase 'new year resolution' appears in a January 1, 1813 Boston newspaper. A 2007 study by Richard Wiseman of about 3,000 people found 88% of resolutions fail.

Script.headline: Resolutions Are 4,000 Years Old
Script.cta: Follow for more things hiding in plain sight.

lines.text: New Year's resolutions are about 4,000 years old.
Around 2000 BC, the Babylonians held a 12-day new year festival called Akitu.
And they made promises to their gods. Pay your debts. Return the farm tools you borrowed.
The Romans kept the habit, making new year promises to Janus, the god with two faces.
The phrase new year resolution shows up in a Boston newspaper in 1813.
And how well do they work? One study of 3,000 people found 88 percent failed.
So we've been breaking the same promises for 4,000 years.
Follow for more things hiding in plain sight.
